content:
Quick answer: Osteoarthritis is usually diagnosed and treated in primary care and community physiotherapy, with referral to orthopaedics if surgery might help. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should be referred urgently to rheumatology, with NICE aiming for referral within 3 working days and treatment within 6 weeks. Gout is mostly managed by your GP, with rheumatology for complex cases.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against NICE guidelines on osteoarthritis (NG226), rheumatoid arthritis (NG100), spondyloarthritis (NG65) and gout (NG219), NICE quality standard QS33, NHS.uk and Welsh Government information on how NICE guidance applies in Wales. Local services are organised differently, so your route may vary.

"Pathway" is NHS shorthand for the route you take through services: who you see first, when you are referred on, and what treatment you can expect along the way. Knowing the usual pathway for your type of arthritis helps you understand where you are, what should come next, and when to push if things stall. This guide simplifies the main arthritis pathways into plain steps.

First: which pathway are you on?

The route depends mainly on whether your arthritis is likely to be:

  • Osteoarthritis, the most common type, usually managed in primary care and community services, with referral to orthopaedics if surgery might help.
  • Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis, which needs prompt referral to rheumatology and long-term specialist-led treatment.
  • Gout, which is mostly diagnosed and treated in primary care, with rheumatology involved for more complex cases.

If you are not sure, ask your GP which they think is most likely and why.

The osteoarthritis pathway

  1. Self-management and pharmacy. Many people start with advice from a pharmacist, staying active and simple pain relief.
  2. Assessment in primary care. You may see a GP or a first contact physiotherapist at your surgery. NICE says osteoarthritis can be diagnosed clinically, without X-rays or scans, in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no more than 30 minutes.
  3. Core treatment. NICE recommends information and support for self-management, therapeutic exercise tailored to you and, where relevant, weight management. NICE also says to offer topical NSAIDs for knee osteoarthritis and consider them for other joints, before considering oral NSAIDs.
  4. Community MSK physiotherapy. Often by self-referral in many areas, or via your GP. You may have individual or group exercise programmes.
  5. Other help as needed. Occupational therapy, podiatry, walking aids, and support with work or daily living.
  6. Referral for surgery, if appropriate. NICE says to consider referral for joint replacement when symptoms substantially affect quality of life and non-surgical treatment is ineffective or unsuitable, using clinical judgement rather than scoring systems. NICE also says people should not be excluded because of age, sex, smoking, other conditions or weight alone.
  7. Surgery and rehabilitation. Pre-operative assessment, the operation, then physiotherapy and recovery at home.

Common sticking points: being told "it's just wear and tear" without an exercise plan, or waiting for a scan that is not needed. If that happens, ask for a referral to physiotherapy or a structured exercise programme. See our waiting list guide for what to do while you wait.

The inflammatory arthritis pathway

For rheumatoid arthritis and similar conditions, speed matters. NICE's quality standard explains that early diagnosis and treatment improves long-term outcomes, physical function and quality of life.

  1. Recognition in primary care. Swollen joints, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, and small joints of the hands or feet being affected are typical warning signs.
  2. Urgent referral. NICE recommends urgent referral for suspected persistent synovitis if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or symptoms have lasted 3 months or more, even if blood tests are normal. Its quality standard says this should happen within 3 working days of seeing a primary care clinician. Blood tests and X-rays should not delay referral.
  3. Specialist assessment. Often in an early inflammatory arthritis clinic. NICE's earlier quality standard said people should be assessed within 3 weeks of referral; this is no longer a formal quality statement but is still considered useful locally.
  4. Diagnosis and starting treatment. NICE's quality standard says adults with active rheumatoid arthritis should start a disease-modifying medicine (cDMARD) within 6 weeks of referral.
  5. Treat to target. NICE recommends monthly checks of CRP and disease activity in specialist care until remission or low disease activity is reached, adjusting treatment as needed.
  6. Advanced treatments if needed. If standard medicines do not control the disease, biologic and targeted medicines may be offered under NICE technology appraisal criteria. See how NHS access to biologics works.
  7. Long-term care. Once stable, monitoring may be shared with your GP. NICE says adults with rheumatoid arthritis should have a named contact in the team, rapid access for flares (advice within 1 working day, according to the quality standard), and an annual review.

For axial spondyloarthritis, NICE's guideline sets out when people with back pain that started before age 45 and lasted more than 3 months should be referred, and recommends that people with confirmed axial spondyloarthritis are referred to a specialist physiotherapist for a structured exercise programme.

The gout pathway

  1. Diagnosis in primary care, based on symptoms and examination, confirmed by a serum urate blood test where possible.
  2. Treating flares with an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of steroids, chosen to suit your other conditions and medicines.
  3. Discussing long-term urate-lowering treatment, such as allopurinol, using a treat-to-target approach with monthly urate checks until the target is reached.
  4. Referral to rheumatology, which NICE says to consider if the diagnosis is uncertain, treatment is not tolerated or not working, or you have more advanced kidney disease or an organ transplant.

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)

PMR causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck and hips, with morning stiffness lasting longer than 45 minutes. The NHS says most people diagnosed are over 65 and it is very rare under 50. The usual route is:

  1. GP assessment, including blood tests such as ESR and CRP, and tests to rule out conditions with similar symptoms, such as rheumatoid arthritis.
  2. Treatment with a steroid called prednisolone, starting at a moderate dose and reduced gradually. The NHS says most people need treatment for 12 months to 2 years.
  3. Possible referral to rheumatology, for example if the diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms do not settle as expected. Ask your GP whether this would help you.

The NHS notes that up to 1 in 5 people with PMR develop temporal arteritis, which needs immediate medical attention. Know the warning signs listed below.

Back pain

Most back pain is not caused by inflammatory arthritis and is managed with advice, staying active and, where needed, physiotherapy. NICE's back pain guideline advises against routine imaging in non-specialist settings. The key thing to look out for is the pattern that suggests axial spondyloarthritis: back pain that started before age 45, has lasted more than 3 months, and has features such as night pain, morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, or a history of psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease or eye inflammation. If that sounds like you, ask your GP about a spondyloarthritis assessment.

Personalised care and your own plan

Whatever your pathway, it helps to have a simple written plan agreed with your clinician: your diagnosis, your treatment, what to do in a flare, who to contact and when your next review is. NICE's spondyloarthritis guideline suggests a flare management plan tailored to the person, and its rheumatoid arthritis guideline stresses rapid access to specialist care for flares. Keep yours somewhere easy to find, and update it after each appointment.

Pain management and other support

Alongside these main routes, you may be referred to:

  • Pain management services or programmes, which focus on improving daily life and coping with persistent pain
  • Occupational therapy, for help with daily tasks, splints, equipment and work
  • Podiatry, for foot problems and footwear
  • NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral in England) for low mood or anxiety
  • Social care, through a needs assessment from your local council, if you need help at home

How pathways differ in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

NICE is an England-based body, and the other nations decide how its guidance applies:

  • Wales: the Welsh Government says NICE guidelines and quality standards are available for use in Wales, although they are generally not mandatory; NICE technology appraisals on medicines have specific funding requirements.
  • Scotland: the Scottish Medicines Consortium, part of Healthcare Improvement Scotland, advises NHS Scotland on new medicines, and SIGN publishes Scottish clinical guidelines. Many NICE recommendations are reflected in practice.
  • Northern Ireland: the Department of Health reviews NICE guidance for local applicability.

The basic clinical steps above are similar across the UK. The biggest differences are in waiting times, how referrals are made and booked, and your rights to choose. Our guide to how NHS referrals work sets out the differences.

Working out where you are on the pathway

Ask your GP or specialist team these questions:

  • What do you think my diagnosis is, and how sure are you?
  • Which service am I being referred to, and is it urgent or routine?
  • What treatment should I be having while I wait?
  • What is the next step after this appointment?
  • Who is my main contact?
  • What would make you refer me on, or bring my appointment forward?

Our full list of questions to ask your consultant covers more situations.

If your pathway has stalled

Signs that things may have stalled include waiting longer than expected with no contact, being bounced between services, or not receiving treatment NICE says you should be offered. Practical steps:

  1. Check the facts. Confirm the referral was sent and received, and where you are on the list.
  2. Update your GP if your symptoms have changed. New information can change your priority.
  3. Use your rights. In England, you can ask to change provider if you are likely to wait more than 18 weeks for consultant-led treatment.
  4. Ask about interim treatment, such as physiotherapy or a change in medicine, while you wait.
  5. Get independent help from PALS in England, PASS in Scotland, Llais in Wales or the Patient and Client Council in Northern Ireland.

When to get medical help

  • Same day (urgent GP appointment or NHS 111): a hot, swollen, very painful joint, especially with a fever; severe headaches with tenderness at the temples, jaw pain when eating or vision problems; or a fever or sore throat while taking an immune-suppressing medicine.
  • A&E or 999: back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals or loss of bladder or bowel control; chest pain or severe breathlessness; sudden loss of vision.
  • Routine GP appointment: symptoms that are gradually getting worse, new joints becoming painful, or treatment that is not helping.

Frequently asked questions

Does everyone with arthritis need to see a specialist?

No. Most osteoarthritis and gout is managed in primary care and community services. Suspected inflammatory arthritis should always be referred to rheumatology.

Why was I sent to physiotherapy instead of a consultant?

For osteoarthritis and most mechanical joint pain, NICE recommends exercise and self-management as core treatment. Community MSK services can also refer you on to a specialist if needed.

How quickly should I be seen for suspected rheumatoid arthritis?

NICE's quality standard says referral should be made within 3 working days of seeing your GP, and treatment with a disease-modifying medicine should start within 6 weeks of referral if you have active disease.

When will I be referred for a joint replacement?

NICE says to consider referral when symptoms substantially affect your quality of life and non-surgical treatment has not worked or is unsuitable. It is a clinical decision, not based on X-ray scores, age or weight alone.

Do NICE guidelines apply in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland?

Not automatically. Wales and Northern Ireland generally use NICE guidance, with local decisions on how it applies. Scotland has its own bodies, including the Scottish Medicines Consortium and SIGN.

What should I do if my care seems stuck?

Check your referral status, update your GP on any changes, ask about treatment while you wait, and use independent advice services such as PALS, PASS, Llais or the Patient and Client Council.
